title: A Good Man Loses Everything
overview: A wealthy, devoted man named Job loses his herds, his servants and all ten of his children in one day, after a challenge in heaven over whether his faith is only a reward for his blessings.

parts.label: Job's good life (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Job lives in Uz, a land outside Israel whose exact location is unknown, and translations call him 'blameless' or 'perfect,' which here means honest and wholehearted rather than sinless. After his children's rounds of feasting, he offers an animal sacrifice for each of them, just in case they had quietly turned against God in their hearts.

parts.label: A meeting in heaven (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: Heavenly beings gather before the LORD (translations say 'angels' or 'sons of God'), and God points out Job to one called 'the satan,' Hebrew for 'the accuser' or 'the adversary.' Christians have long identified this figure with the devil, while many scholars read him here as a kind of prosecutor in God's court, before the later picture of the devil had fully formed.

parts.label: The accuser's challenge (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: The accuser asks whether Job serves God 'for nothing,' suggesting he is good only because God has fenced him in with protection and wealth, and predicts Job will curse God to his face if it is all taken away. God allows him to strike everything Job has, but not Job's own body.

parts.label: Four disasters in one day (vv. 13-19)
parts.note: Raiders called Sabeans and Chaldeans steal the animals and kill the servants, a 'fire of God' burns up the sheep and shepherds (perhaps lightning, though some think a scorching desert wind), and a windstorm brings a house down on all ten of Job's children. The text reports these deaths plainly, one survivor after another, and Job is never told about the scene in heaven.

parts.label: Job mourns and worships (vv. 20-21)
parts.note: Tearing his robe and shaving his head were the usual signs of deep mourning, so Job grieves openly before he falls to the ground and worships. He says he came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing, that the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, and he praises God's name.

parts.label: The narrator's verdict (v. 22)
parts.note: The accuser said Job would curse God, and the Hebrew in verse 11 actually uses the word 'bless' as a softened stand-in for 'curse,' so Job's real blessing in verse 21 answers the challenge with the very same word. The end of verse 22 is translated in different ways: either Job did not accuse God of wrongdoing, or he did nothing foolish or offensive toward God.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read God's role here: some take the heavenly scene as a real account of God allowing evil to test Job for a larger purpose, while others read it as a storytelling frame that raises the question of innocent suffering rather than explaining how God actually works.
think: Do you think a person can be truly good, or truly love someone, without expecting anything in return?
